entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ariaeus, a prominent Persian general active in the late 5th and early 4th centuries BCE, played a pivotal, albeit complex, role in the Achaemenid succession crisis following the death of Darius II. His initial allegiance to Cyrus the Younger, a claimant to the Persian throne, positioned him at the heart of the Battle of Cunaxa in 401 BCE, a conflict that profoundly shaped the military and political landscape of the Near East. Ariaeus's subsequent actions, including his betrayal of the Greek Ten Thousand mercenaries and his involvement in the assassination of the satrap Tissaphernes, underscore the volatile nature of Persian court politics and the shifting loyalties characteristic of the era. His career illuminates the intricate power struggles within the vast Achaemenid Empire and the significant impact of Greek mercenary forces on Persian internal affairs.

At the Battle of Cunaxa in 401 BCE, Ariaeus commanded the left wing of Cyrus the Younger's army, composed primarily of Asian troops, while Cyrus led the formidable Greek mercenary contingent. Following Cyrus's death in battle, Ariaeus became the de facto leader of the remaining Persian forces and, crucially, was offered command of the stranded Greek Ten Thousand. However, his refusal to accept kingship and his subsequent agreement to an armistice with Artaxerxes II, the reigning Achaemenid king, led him to abandon the Greeks. He later participated in the treacherous capture of the Greek generals, a move that forced Xenophon and the remaining Hellenic forces to undertake their epic retreat. Ariaeus subsequently served Artaxerxes II, eventually colluding with Tiribazus to orchestrate the assassination of the powerful satrap Tissaphernes in 395 BCE, a rival whose influence at court threatened their own positions.
